items.title: Blocks and block systems for a group action
The translates of a block partition its orbit
items.strategy: If B is a block and x belongs to gB∩hB, then h^{-1}gB meets B and therefore equals B; hence gB=hB. The distinct translates are therefore disjoint, and their union is the orbit-union of B.

items.title: Block systems are exactly the invariant equivalence relations
items.strategy: Send a block system to the relation 'lie in the same block' and check invariance. Conversely, the equivalence classes of a G-invariant relation form a partition into blocks because classes are either equal or disjoint after translation.

items.title: Primitive and imprimitive transitive actions
Blocks in a finite transitive action have a common size
items.strategy: In a transitive action every block in a given block system is a translate of every other. Restriction of the acting permutation gives bijections between any two translates, so all blocks have the same finite cardinality.

items.title: Blocks containing a point correspond to intermediate subgroups
items.strategy: Identify a transitive G-set with G/G_alpha. For an intermediate subgroup H, its orbit H·alpha is a block. For a block B containing alpha, its setwise stabiliser lies between G_alpha and G and recovers B as its orbit of alpha.

items.title: A transitive action on more than one point is primitive exactly when a point stabilizer is maximal
items.strategy: By the subgroup-block correspondence, nontrivial blocks through alpha are exactly the orbits of intermediate subgroups strictly between G_alpha and G. Therefore no such block exists exactly when G_alpha is maximal.

items.title: A transitive action of prime degree is primitive
items.strategy: Any nonempty block has size dividing the prime degree, because blocks in its block system all have the same size. Therefore a block has size 1 or the whole degree, so only the trivial blocks occur.

items.title: Normal subgroups of a primitive action are transitive or lie in the kernel
items.strategy: For N normal in G, the N-orbits form a G-invariant equivalence relation. In a primitive action they are therefore either the one-block partition or the singleton partition. The singleton case means every element of N fixes every point.

items.title: Regular actions
Abelian normal subgroups of faithful primitive actions are regular
items.strategy: A nontrivial abelian normal subgroup N is transitive by the previous theorem. If n in N fixes one point, then for every point m·alpha in the N-orbit we have n(m·alpha)=m(n·alpha)=m·alpha, so n fixes all points and faithfulness forces n=e.

items.title: k-transitive and k-homogeneous actions
k-transitivity implies k-homogeneity and lower transitivity
items.strategy: A map sending ordered k-tuples sends the underlying k-element subsets, so k-transitivity implies k-homogeneity. To get j-transitivity for j<k, pad the ordered j-tuples by distinct extra points and apply k-transitivity.

items.title: Every doubly transitive action is primitive
items.strategy: In a doubly transitive action the point stabilizer is transitive on the complement of the chosen point. A block containing that point and one other point must therefore contain every other point as well.

items.title: Rank, suborbits, and subdegrees of a transitive action
Orbits on ordered pairs correspond to suborbits
items.strategy: Fix alpha. Send a G-orbit in Omega×Omega to the G_alpha-orbit of its second coordinate in a pair (alpha,beta). This is well-defined because two such pairs differ by an element fixing alpha, and the inverse sends a suborbit Delta to the G-orbit of (alpha,beta) for beta in Delta.

items.title: A transitive action on more than one point is doubly transitive exactly when it has rank two
items.strategy: Rank counts the point-stabilizer orbits. In a transitive action one orbit is always the fixed point itself, so rank two means the stabilizer is transitive on the complement, which is exactly double transitivity.

items.title: Sharply k-transitive actions
A finite sharply k-transitive action has order n(n-1)...(n-k+1)
items.strategy: Fix one ordered k-tuple of distinct points. Sharp k-transitivity gives a bijection between G and the set of ordered k-tuples of distinct points by sending g to the image of the fixed tuple.

items.title: The imprimitive wreath product of permutation groups
A transitive imprimitive action embeds modulo its kernel in an imprimitive wreath product
items.strategy: Let Sigma be the block system through a chosen nontrivial block B, let K be the induced action on Sigma, and let H be the induced action of the block stabilizer on B. After choosing a transversal of blocks, each g in G is encoded by its permutation of Sigma together with the induced permutation on each chosen copy of B. This gives the wreath-product embedding.

items.title: Iwasawa's simplicity criterion for primitive actions
items.strategy: Let N be a nontrivial normal subgroup. Primitivity makes N transitive, so G=N G_alpha. If A is abelian and normal in G_alpha, then every conjugate of A lies in N A; if the conjugates of A generate G, this forces G/N to be abelian and hence G'<=N. A perfect group satisfying the hypotheses is therefore simple.

items.title: The finite Iwasawa criterion
items.strategy: This is the faithful finite specialization of the previous theorem. Once G is perfect, every nontrivial normal subgroup contains G'=G and so equals G.

title: Blocks Primitivity and Multiple Transitivity — Examples

items.title: Blocks in a regular cyclic action are cosets of subgroups
items.strategy: Let C_n act on itself by translation. For each divisor d of n, the cosets of the unique subgroup of order d form a block system; for composite n these are nontrivial blocks, while for prime n only the trivial systems occur.

items.title: The natural actions of symmetric and alternating groups
items.strategy: Record that S_n is sharply n-transitive on {1,...,n} and that A_n is (n-2)-transitive for n>=4. The example displays the page's transitivity hierarchy on the standard permutation groups.

items.title: Affine general linear groups are doubly transitive
items.strategy: On a finite vector space V over F_q, the affine maps x↦Ax+b send any ordered pair of distinct points to any other by first matching differences linearly and then translating the first point.

items.title: Dihedral actions of prime and composite degree
items.strategy: For D_n on the vertices of a regular n-gon, prime n forces primitivity by the prime-degree corollary, while composite n admits nontrivial blocks given by evenly spaced vertices forming smaller regular polygons.

items.title: Projective linear actions and Iwasawa's hypotheses
items.strategy: For PSL_2(F_q) on P^1(F_q), the action is doubly transitive, the stabilizer of infinity contains the translation subgroup x↦x+b as a normal abelian subgroup, and elementary matrices show its conjugates generate the whole group. This is the model application of Iwasawa's criterion.

items.title: The imprimitive wreath product preserves its fiber blocks
items.strategy: For H wr K on B×Sigma, the subsets B×{sigma} are permuted among themselves. This makes the standard fiber decomposition a nontrivial block system whenever both base sets have size greater than one.

items.title: The square-affine group of F_7 is 2-homogeneous but not 2-transitive
items.strategy: Let G={x↦ax+b : a in {1,2,4}, b in F_7}. Because every nonzero class in F_7 is a square or minus a square, G sends any two-element subset to any other. But ordered pairs detect whether the difference is a square, so (0,1) cannot be sent to (0,3).

items.title: FALSE: every transitive action is primitive
items.strategy: Refute with a regular cyclic action of composite degree, whose subgroup cosets are nontrivial blocks.

items.title: FALSE: every block is an invariant subset
items.strategy: A block may be moved disjointly rather than fixed setwise; the vertex pairs in the dihedral action show this explicitly.

items.title: FALSE: every 2-homogeneous action is 2-transitive
items.strategy: Refute with the square-affine action on F_7, which is two-homogeneous on unordered pairs but splits ordered pairs by square and nonsquare differences.

items.title: FALSE: every nontrivial normal subgroup of a faithful primitive group is regular
items.strategy: The valid general conclusion is transitivity. The natural action of S_n has normal subgroup A_n, which is transitive but not free for n>=4.

items.title: FALSE: Iwasawa's criterion needs only transitivity
items.strategy: The proof of Iwasawa's criterion uses primitivity to force nontrivial normal subgroups to be transitive; without primitivity the block kernel can obstruct the argument.

title: Geometric Actions Svarc Milnor and Growth

items.title: Isometric, proper, and cobounded actions on metric spaces
Metric properness agrees with proper discontinuity on proper discrete metric spaces
items.strategy: In a proper discrete metric space, bounded subsets are finite and compact subsets are finite. Transporter finiteness for finite subsets is therefore exactly the usual proper-discontinuity condition.

items.title: Geometric actions on metric spaces
Bounded local displacement on a geodesic space implies coarse Lipschitz control
items.strategy: Subdivide a geodesic segment into pieces of length at most r. If the map moves r-close pairs by at most C, summing over the subdivision gives a linear bound in the total geodesic length.

items.title: Orbit maps of isometric actions are coarse Lipschitz
items.strategy: Choose a finite generating set S and basepoint x. The displacement of each generator at x is bounded, so a word of length n moves x by at most n times the maximum generator displacement.

items.title: Cobounded proper geodesic actions produce finite generating sets
items.strategy: Choose a bounded set B whose G-translates cover X. Properness makes the set of g with B∩gB nonempty finite. A geodesic from x to g·x can be followed through successive translates of B, expressing g as a product of those finitely many transporters.

items.title: The Svarc-Milnor lemma
items.strategy: Use the previous lemma to get a finite generating set from a geometric action. The orbit map is coarsely Lipschitz by generator-displacement bounds, coarsely surjective by coboundedness, and has a linear lower bound by tracing a geodesic through the bounded fundamental set.

items.title: Groups acting geometrically on the same space are quasi-isometric
items.strategy: Each group is quasi-isometric to the common space by the Svarc-Milnor lemma, and quasi-isometry is an equivalence relation.

items.title: The growth function of a finitely generated group
Growth comparison and growth type
Growth comparison is a preorder
items.strategy: Reflexivity is immediate from the defining inequality. For transitivity, compose the two comparison inequalities and absorb the resulting constants into one larger constant.

items.title: Growth type is independent of the finite generating set
items.strategy: Bilipschitz equivalence of the two word metrics controls each word ball between two rescaled balls in the other metric. Translating these ball containments into cardinality bounds gives mutual growth comparison.

items.title: Growth type is a quasi-isometry invariant of finitely generated groups
items.strategy: A quasi-isometry between finitely generated groups is coarsely Lipschitz in both directions. Images and quasi-inverse images of word balls sit inside linearly rescaled balls, and finite generating sets ensure those balls are finite, so the two growth functions mutually dominate.

items.title: Polynomial, subexponential, exponential, and intermediate growth
Free groups of rank at least two have exponential growth
items.strategy: With respect to a free basis, reduced words of length n are counted exactly: 2r choices for the first letter and 2r-1 thereafter. The reduced-word length equals the word length, so the growth function dominates an exponential function when r>=2.

items.title: The homogeneous dimension of a finitely generated nilpotent group
Bass-Guivarch growth-degree formula
Finitely generated nilpotent groups have polynomial growth
items.strategy: Apply the Bass-Guivarch formula and keep only the consequence that the growth function is comparable to a polynomial of the homogeneous dimension.

items.title: Gromov's polynomial-growth theorem
Grigorchuk groups of intermediate growth

title: Geometric Actions Svarc Milnor and Growth — Examples

items.title: The integers act geometrically on the real line
items.strategy: Translations n:x↦x+n are isometries. Properness is immediate from bounded interval transporters, coboundedness from the unit interval, and the orbit map identifies Z with the integer lattice in R.

items.title: Z^n acts geometrically on Euclidean n-space
items.strategy: Integer translations on R^n are isometric, proper, and cobounded by the unit cube. The Svarc-Milnor lemma therefore identifies Z^n with Euclidean n-space up to quasi-isometry.

items.title: Free groups act geometrically on regular trees
items.strategy: The Cayley graph of a free group with respect to a free basis is a tree, and left translation acts freely, properly, and cocompactly on it. The orbit map is the inclusion of vertices.

items.title: Horizontal translations of Z on the Euclidean plane are proper but not cobounded
items.strategy: Let n act on R^2 by (x,y)↦(x+n,y). Bounded sets have only finitely many transporting integers, but every orbit stays in one horizontal line, so points with large |y| escape every bounded neighbourhood of a fixed orbit.

items.title: Free abelian groups have polynomial growth of the expected degree
items.strategy: For the standard basis of Z^n, l^1-balls are sandwiched between cubes of side proportional to R, so their cardinalities are bounded above and below by constant multiples of R^n. Comparing n=1 and n>=2 separates linear and higher-degree polynomial growth.

items.title: The discrete Heisenberg group has growth degree four
items.strategy: Present the discrete Heisenberg group on triples $(a,b,c)inmathbb Z^3$, compute directly that its commutator subgroup is central and that the first and second lower-central quotients have free ranks two and one, and then apply the Bass-Guivarch formula $1cdot 2 + 2cdot 1 = 4$.

items.title: Quasi-isometry without bounded geometry need not preserve local ball counts
items.strategy: Attach n leaves by unit edges to the integer vertex n on a bi-infinite line. Collapsing each finite leaf cluster to its spine vertex is a quasi-isometry onto Z, but radius-one balls at the vertices n have size n+3 in the comb space and size 3 in Z.

items.title: FALSE: a proper isometric action has bounded orbits
items.strategy: Refute with the translation action of Z on the real line, whose orbits are unbounded.

items.title: FALSE: cobounded and cocompact are identical without extra hypotheses
items.strategy: Refute with the trivial action on the open interval (0,1): the single orbit is cobounded because the space has finite diameter, but the quotient is not compact.

items.title: FALSE: the growth function is independent of the generating set pointwise
items.strategy: Compare Z with generators {±1} and {±1,±2}: the exact ball counts differ although the growth type is the same.

items.title: FALSE: every subexponential growth group has polynomial growth
items.strategy: Refute with Grigorchuk's groups, whose growth is intermediate.

items.title: FALSE: Gromov's polynomial-growth theorem is proved on this page
items.strategy: The page records Gromov's theorem as an external result and does not supply a local proof.
